title: Privacy
description: Seclusion from unwanted attention or disclosure
wiki_lead:
Privacy (English pronunciation: /ˈprɪvəsi/, English pronunciation: /ˈpraɪvəsi/) is the condition or claim of an individual or group to be free from unwanted access, observation or disclosure, and to determine for themselves how far they, and information about them, are exposed to others. The concept has no single accepted definition. Lawyers, philosophers and social scientists have variously understood it as a right to be let alone, as limited access to the self, as secrecy, as control over personal information, as a precondition of personhood and intimate relationships, and as the appropriate flow of information within social contexts.
Distinctions between public and private life are found in many ancient societies and religious traditions, but privacy emerged as a distinct legal claim only in the nineteenth century, when new printing and photographic technologies and the popular press prompted calls for legal protection. In the second half of the twentieth century the spread of computers shifted attention from intrusion and publicity towards the collection and processing of personal data, producing a body of data protection law that began in Western Europe in the 1970s and has since spread worldwide.
Privacy is protected as a human right by Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and regional instruments such as Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Many national constitutions protect it expressly, and courts in other countries have derived it from broader guarantees. The structure of protection nevertheless differs markedly between jurisdictions: European law tends to treat privacy as an aspect of personal dignity and regulates the processing of personal data comprehensively, whereas law in the United States has traditionally emphasised liberty against the state and regulates the private sector by sector.
The Internet, mobile phones and large-scale data analysis have intensified debate about surveillance by governments and corporations, the commercial use of personal data, and the extent to which individuals can meaningfully control information about themselves. Responses include legislation, litigation, and privacy-enhancing technologies such as encryption and anonymity tools.
Privacy overlaps with, but is distinct from, security: information security concerns the protection of data against unauthorised access, whereas privacy also concerns whether data should be collected and used at all, and for what purposes. Privacy may also take the form of bodily integrity and protection of the home and person against physical intrusion. In many legal systems, protection of digital privacy has developed as an extension of the older right to privacy, supplemented by legislation regulating both public and private bodies.

Etymology

The English word privacy is derived from private, which comes from the Latin privatus, "set apart (from what is public), belonging to oneself (not to the state)". Privatus is the perfect passive participle of the verb prīvō (infinitive prīvāre), "to bereave, deprive" and also "to free, release", which is itself derived from privus, "one's own, individual".


Conceptions of privacy

Scholars have long observed that privacy is a contested and internally diverse concept. Daniel J. Solove describes it as "a concept in disarray" and groups the main theoretical accounts into six families: the right to be let alone, limited access to the self, secrecy, control over personal information, personhood, and intimacy. Each captures some privacy problems while failing to account for others, which has led Solove and others to favour pluralistic or contextual accounts over a single definition.


The right to be let alone
In "The Right to Privacy" (1890), the Boston lawyers Samuel D. Warren and Louis Brandeis argued that the common law should recognise a general "right to be let alone", a phrase they took from Judge Thomas M. Cooley. Their immediate concern was that "instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise" had "invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life", a reference to the sensationalist press of the period, often described as yellow journalism. They grounded the right not in property or contract but in the protection of an "inviolate personality".
The formula proved influential but indeterminate, since it does not explain which forms of being left alone the law should protect. It has been read to include a person's right to choose seclusion from the attention of others, and to be free from scrutiny or observation in private settings such as the home. Although the concept did not define privacy precisely enough to ground comprehensive legal protection, it strengthened the notion of an individual right to privacy and began a long tradition of debate about such rights in the United States.


Limited access
A second family of theories treats privacy as limited accessibility to the self. In 1890 the American journalist E. L. Godkin described private life as "the right of every man to keep his affairs to himself, and to decide for himself to what extent they shall be the subject of public observation and discussion". Ruth Gavison developed the idea analytically, arguing that privacy concerns the extent to which a person is known to others (secrecy), the subject of their attention (anonymity) and physically accessible to them (solitude). Sissela Bok similarly defined privacy as "the condition of being protected from unwanted access by others—either physical access, personal information, or attention".


Secrecy
On a narrower view, privacy is the concealment of discreditable or sensitive information. Richard Posner described it as the right of people to "conceal information about themselves that others might use to their disadvantage", and argued on economic grounds that such concealment can amount to a form of misrepresentation that impairs the efficient working of markets. When privacy is understood as secrecy, it is usually imagined as a selective secrecy, in which individuals keep some information private while choosing to make other information public. Critics reply that the secrecy view cannot explain why a person may retain a privacy interest in information that has already been disclosed to some people, or in information that is not discreditable at all.


Control over personal information
The most influential definition in the information age is that of the political scientist Alan Westin, for whom privacy is "the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others". The philosopher Charles Fried likewise argued that privacy "is not simply an absence of information about us in the minds of others; rather it is the control we have over information about ourselves". The control model underlies the fair information practice principles on which most data protection legislation is built. It has been criticised for presupposing that individuals are able to make informed choices about complex and opaque data practices.
The psychologist Carl A. Johnson tied privacy to the psychological concept of "personal control", which he modelled as a process with four stages and two kinds of behaviour–outcome relationship, the outcomes depending on both situational and personal factors. On this model, privacy consists of "behaviors falling at specific locations on these two dimensions". The four stages are outcome choice control, the selection between possible outcomes; behaviour selection control, the selection between strategies for attaining the chosen outcome; outcome effectance, the carrying out of the chosen behaviour so as to achieve the outcome; and outcome realisation control, the person's interpretation of the outcome achieved. The two dimensions are primary control, in which behaviour directly causes outcomes, and secondary control, in which it does so indirectly. Johnson treated privacy as behaviour exercising secondary control over outcomes, and argued that a person's conception of privacy itself depends on these behaviour–outcome relationships; he developed the account in dialogue with the work of Irwin Altman, and of Maxine Wolfe and Robert S. Laufer.
The philosopher Lorenzo Magnani extends the idea of control to personal identity. He argues that consciousness is partly constituted by external representations of the self, such as narratives and data stored outside the body, but that much of it consists of internal representations that remain private and are rarely externalised. Magnani describes this internal privacy as a form of "information property" or "moral capital" that is essential to free choice and personal agency. When too much of a person's identity is externalised and subjected to scrutiny, he contends, the result is a loss of control, dignity and responsibility; the protection of privacy therefore safeguards the ability to pursue personal projects free from intrusive external forces.


Contextual integrity

Helen Nissenbaum's theory of contextual integrity holds that privacy is violated not by disclosure as such but by information flows that breach the norms of the social context in which the information was shared. A patient's disclosure of symptoms to a doctor is appropriate within medicine but would violate contextual norms if passed to an employer. The theory has been widely adopted in computer science and policy analysis because it explains why aggregating individually public information can nevertheless be harmful.


Personhood, autonomy and personal growth
Privacy may be understood as a prerequisite for the development of a sense of self-identity. Privacy barriers, in particular, are instrumental in this process. According to Irwin Altman, such barriers "define and limit the boundaries of the self" and thus "serve to help define [the self]." This control primarily entails the ability to regulate contact with others. Control over the "permeability" of the self's boundaries enables one to control what constitutes the self and thus to define what is the self.
Several philosophers present privacy as a condition for the development of personhood. Jeffrey Reiman argued that privacy is a social ritual by which a society recognises, and conveys to the individual—that one's physical existence is under one's moral ownership. Hence, a moral right to self-determination devirated from the notion of privacy. Stanley Benn grounded privacy in respect for persons as choosers, observing that covert observation alters the conditions under which a person chooses without one's knowledge. Joseph Kupfer linked privacy to the formation of an autonomous self-concept, drawing on studies of child development and on Erving Goffman's account of "total institutions", in which the systematic deprivation of privacy erodes inmates' sense of self. In his understanding, an autonomous self-concept entails a conception of oneself as a "purposeful, self-determining, responsible agent" and an awareness of one's capacity to control the boundary between self and other—that is, to control who can access and experience one's and to which extent. In United States constitutional law, a related "decisional" conception of privacy protected choices about contraception, abortion and intimate relationships.
In addition, privacy may be seen as a state that fosters personal growth, a process integral to the development of self-identity. Hyman Gross suggested that, without privacy—solitude, anonymity, and temporary releases from social roles—individuals would be unable to freely express themselves and to engage in self-discovery and self-criticism. Such self-discovery and self-criticism contributes to one's understanding of oneself and shapes one's sense of identity.


Intimacy
In a way analogous to how the personhood theory imagines privacy as some essential part of being
grok_lead: Privacy is the normative claim that individuals and groups have authority over aspects of their lives shielded from intrusive observation, judgment, or interference by others, encompassing bodily privacy, communications privacy, control over personal information, intimate decisions, bodily integrity, and spatial seclusion. This concept, rooted in respect for human dignity and autonomy, enables psychological well-being, trust in social relations, and protection against harms like exploitation or coercion, as empirical studies link privacy violations to heightened stress and reduced interpersonal cooperation. Philosophically, it draws from first principles of limited access to one's inner sphere, distinct from but overlapping with liberty, while legally it manifests as protections against arbitrary state or private incursions, without implying absolute seclusion. Historically, modern privacy discourse crystallized in the late 19th century amid technological advances like photography and mass media, with Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis articulating it as "the right to be let alone" in response to invasive journalism, influencing subsequent jurisprudence. In the 20th century, this evolved into constitutional dimensions, such as implied rights in the U.S. Bill of Rights against unreasonable searches, extended through cases affirming decisional privacy in reproduction and family matters, though courts consistently balanced it against compelling public interests like security. Globally, frameworks like the European Convention on Human Rights (Article 8) and statutes such as the U.S. Privacy Act of 1974 codified limits on data handling by governments, prioritizing individual control over records to prevent abuse. In the digital era, privacy faces empirical strains from pervasive data aggregation by corporations and states, where algorithms process vast personal datasets for prediction and targeting, often yielding conveniences like personalized services but enabling risks such as identity theft âdocumented in breaches affecting billionsâor discriminatory profiling, as meta-analyses confirm privacy concerns erode trust and behavioral intentions toward technology adopters. Defining controversies include trade-offs with national security, as post-9/11 surveillance expansions demonstrated measurable intelligence gains alongside overreach complaints, and debates over consent in "free" services, where users trade data for access amid asymmetric power dynamics. These tensions underscore privacy's non-absolute nature: causal analyses reveal that while strong protections foster innovation and equity, excessive restrictions can hinder societal benefits like fraud detection or epidemiological modeling, necessitating context-specific calibrations informed by verifiable outcomes rather than ideological priors.
